example.problem: The bill is $48.50 before tip. You want to leave 15% and split the total between 2 people. How much does each person pay?
steps: Add it to the bill: $48.50 + $7.28 = $55.78 total.
example.title: Dinner for two

faqs.a: In the US, 15% is the standard minimum for sit-down service, 18 to 20% is typical for good service, and above 20% for exceptional service. Takeout and counter service usually get less, around 5 to 10%.
faqs.q: What is a good tip percentage?

faqs.a: Find 10% by moving the decimal point one place left, then add half of that for 5%. On $48.50, 10% is $4.85 and 5% is about $2.43, so 15% is about $7.28.
faqs.q: How do I work out 15% of a bill in my head?

faqs.a: No. The standard is to calculate the tip on the pre-tax subtotal. Most bills show the subtotal separately so you can use that number.
faqs.q: Should I tip on the tax too?

faqs.a: Split each person's share proportionally: add up what everyone ordered, divide each person's amount by that subtotal, and multiply each fraction by the tipped total. The calculator's even split works when everyone ordered about the same.
faqs.q: How do we split fairly if one person ordered much more?

formula.expr: each pays = total ÷ number of people
formula.label: Per person

howItWorks: A tip is just a percentage of the bill. The calculator turns your percent into a decimal by dividing by 100, multiplies it by the bill to get the tip amount, and adds it back to the bill for the total. If you are splitting, it divides that total by the number of people.

These are simple estimates for everyday restaurant math, not financial advice. Local tipping customs vary: 15 to 20 percent is standard for sit-down restaurants in the US, while some places add a service charge automatically, so check the bill first to avoid tipping twice.
intro: Work out how much to leave as a tip, what the bill comes to in total, and how much each person pays when you split it. Enter the bill before the tip, pick a percentage, and set how many people are sharing.

mistakes.text: Convention is to tip on the bill before tax is added, not on the after-tax total. On a $50 bill with $4 tax, 20% should be $10 (20% of 50), not $10.80 (20% of 54).
mistakes.title: Tipping on the total instead of the pre-tax bill

mistakes.text: Some restaurants, especially for large groups, add an automatic service charge of 18 to 20%. Check the itemized bill before adding a tip on top, or you will pay twice.
mistakes.title: Forgetting a service charge is already included

mistakes.text: When $48.50 at 15% gives $7.275, rounding to $7.28 is fair. Rounding down to $7 every time quietly shrinks the tip below the percentage you intended.
mistakes.title: Rounding the tip down badly

mistakes.text: Add the tip first, then split the total. Splitting the bill and tipping on your own share only can short-change the server if shares are uneven.
mistakes.title: Splitting before adding the tip
